title: {{NAME}} and the Invisible Referee
moral: When you play with honesty and heart, the game is always worth playing.

pages.content:
{{NAME}} scored the goal that won the local cup and felt nothing but guilty.

Because he had seen something nobody else had: a tiny fairy on the goal line, no bigger than a finger, who had stuck her foot out and deflected the ball exactly one centimetre to the right of the keeper's dive.

The cup was in his hands. The crowd was cheering. The fairy was sitting on the goalpost crossbar, eating a sunflower seed and looking pleased with herself.

{{NAME}} put the cup down.

pages.content:
He got to her at half time by walking very casually to the goalpost and pretending to check his boot.

"You deflected my shot," he said, very quietly.

"I levelled the pitch," she said. "Their goalkeeper got a lucky bounce in the semi-final. I balance things. That is my job."

"That's not how football works," said {{NAME}}.

"It's how fair works," she said. "Which is more important?"

This was an unexpectedly difficult question.

pages.content:
He thought about it through the second half.

On one hand: the goal had technically gone in. On the other hand: he'd felt the deflection. On the third hand (if he had one): the other team had gotten a lucky bounce.

He played the rest of the match very hard and very honestly, leaving the fairy out of it entirely.

With one minute left, he found himself one-on-one with the keeper. He could see the fairy on the crossbar, watching. He looked away from her.

He shot. Top corner. No help needed.

pages.content:
After the match, the fairy landed on his hand.

"That second goal was all yours," she said.

"I know," said {{NAME}}. "That's the point."

She cocked her head. "You'd rather score honestly than win with help?"

"If I win with help I didn't really prove anything," he said. "I proved I can win with help. That's not the same thing."

The fairy was quiet for a moment. Then she said: "You're the first player who's ever said that to me."

pages.content:
She was gone by the time he got his medal.

{{NAME}} walked home with the medal around his neck and his second goal replaying in his head: the moment before the shot when he looked away from the crossbar and decided to do it himself.

That was the goal he'd remember. Not the first one.

In bed that night, the medal on his pillow beside him, he stared at the ceiling and smiled.

Somewhere outside, very faintly, he heard a sound like a tiny pair of hands clapping.
